summary: Describes how to split MPEG video and audio streams into packets for real-time transport over RTP. It replaces RFC 2038.

plainLanguage.summary: MPEG video is compressed in a way that assumes it will arrive without errors, which is not true of the Internet. This document explains how to cut an MPEG stream into RTP packets, and how to mark those packets so a receiver can pick up the stream again after losing one.

subtitle: How to slice MPEG video and audio into RTP packets so they can be streamed over IP networks.

tldr.problem: MPEG streams are designed for a reliable, error-free medium such as a disc or a broadcast link, and they do not fit the packet sizes an IP network uses.
tldr.mechanism: The document defines two ways to carry MPEG in RTP. One keeps the MPEG system layer and only adds framing, the other puts the compressed video and audio straight into RTP packets with a small header that says where slices begin and end.
tldr.outcome: A receiver can find the start of the next slice after a lost packet and resynchronise, so one dropped packet does not spoil the rest of the stream. The document replaced RFC 2038 in 1998.

facts.label: Audio-specific header
facts.value: 32 bits: 16 unused bits and a 16-bit fragment offset

today: RFC 2250 is a Proposed Standard on the IETF Standards Track. It replaced RFC 2038 in 1998, with the packet loss resilience mechanisms extended to carry the extra picture header information MPEG-2 needs, and it has not itself been obsoleted or updated.

sections.title: Two Ways to Carry MPEG over RTP
sections.content:
The MPEG1 and MPEG2 standards define compressed video and audio, and a system layer that multiplexes them with timing information. Those system formats were built for disc storage and broadcast links. This document describes a packetization scheme that carries such a stream over the Real-time Transport Protocol (RTP).

It defines two payload formats. The first, in Section 2, keeps the MPEG system layer and carries MPEG1 System streams, MPEG2 Transport Streams and MPEG2 Program Streams. It aims at maximum interoperability with MPEG System environments. The second, in Section 3, drops the system layer altogether and puts the compressed data itself, which MPEG calls an Elementary Stream, straight into RTP packets. It aims at maximum compatibility with other RTP media streams.

The document targets interoperability among four kinds of end system: a Transmitting Interworking Unit that receives MPEG from a native transport stream system, a Receiving Interworking Unit that forwards received MPEG to one, a Transmitting Internet End-System that holds or generates MPEG itself, and a Receiving Internet End-System that plays what it receives.
sections.plainLanguage: There are two ways to send MPEG over a network. One keeps the MPEG system's own packaging and adds network framing around it. The other throws that packaging away and puts the compressed data straight into network packets, which suits the Internet better.

sections.title: MPEG System and Transport Streams over RTP
sections.content:
Each RTP packet carries a timestamp taken from the sender's 90 kHz clock reference. That clock is synchronised to the system's Program Clock Reference or System Clock Reference, and the timestamp marks the target transmission time of the first byte of the payload. It is not the media display timestamp, and it is never passed to the MPEG decoder. Its purposes are to estimate and reduce network-induced jitter and to synchronise relative time drift between transmitter and receiver.

For MPEG2 Transport Streams the payload holds a whole number of MPEG transport packets. To avoid end-system inefficiencies, several small transport packets, normally fixed at 188 bytes, are aggregated into one RTP packet, and the count is obtained by dividing the payload length by 188. MPEG2 Program Streams and MPEG1 system streams have no packetization restrictions and are treated as a packetized stream of bytes.

The RTP header is used as follows. A distinct payload type is assigned to each of MPEG1 System Streams, MPEG2 Program Streams and MPEG2 Transport Streams. The M bit is set to 1 whenever the timestamp is discontinuous, for example when a sender switches from one data source to another, so that mixers and translators synchronising to the flow can ignore the difference. The timestamp is a 32-bit 90 kHz value for the target transmission time of the first byte of the packet.
sections.plainLanguage: Each packet is stamped with the time the first byte should be sent, using a 90 kHz clock that tracks the MPEG system's own clock. The stamp is for measuring jitter and drift, not for playback. Transport stream packets are small, so several are gathered into one RTP packet.

sections.title: MPEG Elementary Streams and Fragmentation Rules
sections.content:
Four elementary stream types may be carried directly in RTP: MPEG1 Video, MPEG2 Video, MPEG1 Audio and MPEG2 Audio. A distinct payload type is assigned to video and to audio. Whether the data is MPEG1 or MPEG2 need not be signalled, because the elementary stream headers themselves say so: MPEG2 Video follows its sequence header with a sequence extension, and MPEG1 Audio differs from MPEG2 Audio in its ancillary data header.

Presentation Time Stamps of 32 bits with 90 kHz accuracy are carried in the fixed RTP header, and all packets making up one picture or audio frame share the same timestamp.

Since MPEG pictures are large they are normally fragmented into packets smaller than a typical network MTU. Three placement rules apply. A Video Sequence Header, when present, is always at the beginning of an RTP payload. A GOP header, when present, is at the beginning of the payload or follows a Video Sequence Header. A Picture Header, when present, is at the beginning of the payload or follows a GOP header. Each elementary stream header must be completely contained within one packet, so a minimum RTP payload size of 261 bytes must be supported to hold the largest single header, the extension data header containing the quant matrix extension.

In MPEG each picture is made up of one or more slices, and a slice is the intended unit of recovery from loss. The beginning of a slice must either be the first data in a packet or follow an integral number of slices in that packet, so that the start of the next slice can be found without scanning the packet.
sections.plainLanguage: The rules about where headers sit inside a packet exist so a receiver can find its way after a loss. Each header starts a packet, so a missing packet is easy to spot. A slice is the unit a decoder recovers at, so each packet also says where slices begin and end.

sections.title: The MPEG Video-Specific Header
sections.content:
The MPEG video-specific header is attached to every RTP packet after the fixed RTP header and is 32 bits long. The first four bits are unused and must be set to zero.

The T bit says whether the MPEG-2 header extension follows. The TR field holds the 10-bit temporal reference of the current picture within the current GOP; it ranges from 0 to 1023 and is constant for all packets of a given picture. The AN and N bits carry error resilience information for MPEG-2: AN marks that N is in use, and N is set to 1 when the picture header information previously sent cannot be used to rebuild a header for the current picture, for instance because it was encoded with different parameters. N must be constant for all packets of the same picture. The S bit is normally 0 and is set to 1 at each MPEG sequence header. The B and E bits mark the beginning and the end of an MPEG slice. The P field gives the picture type: I (1), P (2), B (3) or D (4), constant for a given picture, with 000 forbidden and 101 to 111 reserved.

The remaining four fields, full_pel_backward_vector, backward_f_code, full_pel_forward_vector and forward_f_code, are copied from the most recent picture header and are constant for a given picture. For I frames none of them are present in the picture header and they must be set to zero; for P frames only the last two are present and the first two must be zero; for B frames all four are present.
sections.plainLanguage: The 32-bit video header tells a receiver what it needs to resynchronise: which picture this is, whether the header information has changed, and where the slices start and stop. The picture type is in there too, so the receiver knows whether the picture can be decoded on its own.

sections.title: The MPEG-2 Video Header Extension
sections.content:
The optional MPEG-2 video-specific header extension is another 32 bits, present when the T bit is set. Its first bit is unused and must be zero. The E bit says that one or more extensions follow: the quant matrix extension, the picture display extension, the picture temporal scalable extension, the picture spatial scalable extension or the copyright extension. The first byte of that data gives the length in 32-bit words including the length field itself, and zero padding aligns it to a 32-bit boundary. Because these extensions may not be vital to decoding a picture, including any one of them is optional even when the extension header itself is present.

The rest of the header carries motion vector codes and picture coding flags copied from the most recent picture coding extension: four f_code values for the forward and backward horizontal and vertical vectors, the intra DC precision, the picture structure, and single-bit flags for top field first, frame predicted frame DCT, concealment motion vectors, q_scale type, intra VLC format, alternate scan, repeat first field, chroma 420 type, progressive frame, and a composite display flag that makes 32 further bits of composite display information follow.
sections.plainLanguage: This extra 32 bits is optional. It carries the details MPEG-2 adds about a picture, such as motion prediction codes. When it is present, the receiver has more to work with when it has to rebuild a lost picture header.

sections.title: The MPEG Audio-Specific Header
sections.content:
The MPEG audio-specific header is attached at the start of the payload of an MPEG1 or MPEG2 Audio payload type, after any RTP headers. It is 32 bits long: the first 16 bits are unused and must be zero, and the second 16 bits hold the byte offset into the audio frame for the data in this packet.

Audio frames may be packed several to a packet, in which case the packet must contain an integral number of audio frames and the fragmentation header must be set to 0. The offset is needed when a single frame is too large for one packet and must be split. The document's example is Layer-II MPEG audio sampled at 44.1 kHz, where a frame represents 26.1 milliseconds; at a compressed bit rate of 384 kbit/s the average frame is 1.25 kBytes, so with 500-byte packets each frame straddles three RTP packets. The audio fragmentation indicator header must be present for an MPEG1 or MPEG2 Audio payload type to allow this.
sections.plainLanguage: Audio gets a small header too, with a number that says how far into the audio frame this packet starts. It is needed because one audio frame is often bigger than a packet, so a frame can be spread over several packets.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Packets using this payload format are subject to the security considerations of the RTP specification and of any applicable RTP profile. Confidentiality of the media streams is achieved by encryption. Because the data compression is applied end to end, encryption may be performed after compression, so the two operations do not conflict.

There is a potential denial-of-service threat against encodings whose receiver-side processing cost varies with the data, since an attacker could inject packets that are expensive to decode. The document notes that this encoding does not show any significant non-uniformity. As with any IP-based protocol, a receiver may also be overloaded simply by receiving too many packets, whether wanted or unwanted. Network-layer authentication may be used to discard packets from undesired sources, although the cost of that authentication may itself be high, and pruning of specific sources may be implemented in future versions of IGMP and in multicast routing protocols so that a receiver can select which sources may reach it. The security review found no additional considerations beyond those in the RTP specification.
sections.plainLanguage: Encrypting the media is what protects it, and it can be done after compression. The document also checks the format for denial-of-service weaknesses and finds none worth reporting beyond what RTP itself already has.

sections.title: Error Recovery and Resynchronization
sections.content:
Appendix 1 of the document offers error recovery and resynchronization strategies as guidelines only. A compliant receiver is free to use other strategies, or none.

When decoding starts, the receiver may discard packets until the sequence-header-present bit is set, because from that point the stream carries enough state for an MPEG decoder to work. Loss of packets holding a GOP header or a picture header shows up as an unexpected change in the temporal reference and picture type. Two counters, one for reference pictures and one for dependent pictures, are incremented together and matched against the temporal reference of each arriving picture; a mismatch means a header was lost. A lost GOP header can then be rebuilt using a null time code, the closed GOP flag repeated from earlier GOP headers, and the broken link flag set to 1.

When a packet is lost, signalled by a gap in the RTP sequence number, the receiver may discard packets until the beginning-of-slice bit is set. At that point there is enough state to decode from the next slice boundary, possibly after the GOP header or picture header has been reconstructed. If the information needed for reconstruction is not available from any source, the recommendation is to delete data until a new picture start code appears.
sections.plainLanguage: After losing a packet, a receiver can work out what it missed by watching the picture numbers change unexpectedly. It can then rebuild the missing header, or skip forward to the start of the next slice and carry on from there.

viz.caption: THE PLACEMENT RULES FOR MPEG HEADERS

items.title: Sequence header
items.text: Always at the beginning of an RTP payload, when present.

items.title: GOP header
items.text: At the beginning of the payload, or after a video sequence header.

items.title: Picture header
items.text: At the beginning of the payload, or after a GOP header.

items.title: Slices
items.text: A slice starts either as the first data in a packet or after a whole number of slices, so a receiver can find the next one without scanning.

items.title: Minimum payload
items.text: 261 bytes, enough for the largest single elementary stream header.

fields.name: MBZ
fields.desc: Unused. Must be set to zero.

fields.name: TR
fields.desc: Temporal reference of the current picture in the current GOP, from 0 to 1023.

fields.name: AN
fields.desc: The N bit is used to signal changes in the MPEG-2 picture header information.

fields.name: N
fields.desc: New picture header: the previously sent picture header cannot rebuild this one.

fields.name: P
fields.desc: Picture type: I (1), P (2), B (3) or D (4).

fields.name: BFC
fields.desc: backward_f_code from the most recent picture header.

fields.name: FFC
fields.desc: forward_f_code from the most recent picture header.

fields.name: FBV
fields.desc: full_pel_backward_vector from the most recent picture header.

fields.name: X
fields.desc: Unused. Must be set to zero.

fields.name: D
fields.desc: Composite display flag; 32 further bits of composite display information follow.

fields.name: MBZ
fields.desc: Unused. Must be set to zero.

fields.name: Frag_offset
fields.desc: Byte offset into the audio frame for the data in this packet.
